A curious engineer.

How I got here

I started college wanting to be a web developer. Hardware changed that. While retaking Digital Logic and EE 201, I discovered how satisfying it is to watch an abstract idea become a circuit that behaves exactly as designed, and computer architecture and embedded systems courses made that interest stick.

Where I'm headed

I want to work in hardware research, designing and verifying digital systems, including the kind of machine-learning hardware I've begun to explore in CPRE 4870. I also know my own gap: I can finish a lab, but I want the judgment to design a system from a blank page. That is why I'm building personal projects, like the FPGA Tetris game I have just started (listed on my résumé page), outside of coursework.

Quick facts

  • Major Computer Engineering, B.S., Iowa State University
  • Expected graduation December 2026
  • Focus Hardware design, and machine-learning hardware
  • Code github.com/devjwk

Senior Design

Odyssey · Team SDDec26-08 · CPRE 4910 / 4920

ClientISU Adventure Rec Program
Team6 students; my team role is full stack
StackHTML/CSS/JavaScript, Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, Nginx
SecurityJWT authentication, bcrypt password hashing, role-based access
HostingUbuntu VM behind an Nginx reverse proxy (development server at sddec26-08.ece.iastate.edu)

Description of project

Odyssey is a centralized trip-management website for the ISU Adventure Rec Program. Before it, trip planning was manual and spread across many spreadsheets, waiver and payment coordination was outdated, and there was no single system. Odyssey lets students register for trips online and submit their information, and gives staff one place to plan trips and manage participants.

The site has four kinds of users: travelers browse and register for trips; trip leaders see the roster for their trips, including dietary, medical, and emergency contact information; organization leaders create and edit trips and manage leaders; and admins create organizations and assign their leaders. Security requirements include hashed passwords, JWT-protected API routes, role-based authorization, medical and emergency data stored separately from accounts, and database constraints that block duplicate registrations.

My role

My team role is full stack. I presented the project's task decomposition, system architecture, and backend design to the Senior Design panel. I work on the Node.js/Express backend, which is organized into routes, controllers, and JWT and role-check middleware, and on connecting it to the frontend pages.

Skills or knowledge gained

  • Organizing a REST API by feature, with routes separated from controllers, so the team can add features without rewriting the server
  • Protecting an app in layers: Nginx routing with rate limiting, JWT authentication, and page-level role checks
  • Using database constraints and a relational schema (users, organizations, programs, registrations, leaders) to enforce rules such as no duplicate sign-ups
  • Testing a backend with Postman, Jest, and Supertest, and checking database behavior such as cascading deletes directly in pgAdmin
  • Working in parallel: each developer pushes a branch to GitLab that is deployed on the shared VM to its own route and port

Status and next steps

At the end of the first semester, Odyssey delivers the core of trip management: registration, organization tools, and secure user access. Next semester's goals are notifications, integrated waiver and payment management, reporting for organizations, user testing with Adventure Program members, separate development and production machines, and SSL with a routable domain.

Supporting documents

  • Project repository on ISU GitLab: git.ece.iastate.edu/sd/sddec26-08
  • Senior Design panel presentation: slides are on the Experience and presentations page

Big picture contribution

Odyssey replaces the Adventure Program's spreadsheets and manual coordination with one system. The backend I work on is what turns each role's pages into working features: it decides who can see or change what, and it keeps registrations consistent.

Three RISC-V processors in VHDL

CourseCPRE 3810, October – December 2025
Team2 people (Project Group F_04)
StackVHDL, RISC-V assembly, QuestaSim, Quartus (timing), RARS, the course toolflow
ResultHardware-scheduled pipeline finishes Mergesort about 20% faster than single-cycle

Description of project

We built the same RISC-V (RV32I) processor three ways and measured each against the same Mergesort benchmark. The single-cycle design is simple, but one instruction passes through every block per clock, so the slowest instruction sets the period. The software-scheduled pipeline splits the datapath into five stages for a much faster clock, but the programmer must reorder code and insert NOPs by hand. The hardware-scheduled pipeline adds forwarding, stall, and flush logic so unmodified programs run correctly.

Single-cycle
41.4 ns
Software-scheduled pipeline
16.8 ns
Hardware-scheduled pipeline
25.43 ns
Show the data table
DesignClock periodCPIMergesort time
Single-cycle41.40 nsabout 1.0070,214 ns
Software-scheduled pipeline16.80 ns1.1274,105 ns
Hardware-scheduled pipeline25.43 ns1.3156,327 ns

The result that surprised me: the software-scheduled pipeline has the fastest clock but loses on Mergesort, because scheduling grows the program from 1,695 to 3,948 executed instructions. A faster clock only helps if the extra work it creates is smaller than the gain.

My role

  • Single-cycle: the control unit (built from an instruction-by-signal table), the fetch logic rewritten to support jalr, ALU and datapath integration, and testbenches for the control unit and ALU.
  • Software-scheduled pipeline: the four pipeline registers (IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB), top-level integration, and rescheduled test programs.
  • Hardware-scheduled pipeline: the forwarding unit, the load-use stall and branch-flush logic, pipeline registers with stall and flush inputs, twelve module-level testbenches, a coverage table of producer and consumer instruction pairs, and the benchmarks.
  • My teammate and I wrote the reports together.

Skills or knowledge gained

  • Turning a table of instructions and control signals into decode logic and checking it with a testbench before integration
  • Separating hazards that forwarding can fix from those that need a stall, and deciding what to stall or flush for each kind of jump
  • Building a systematic hazard test plan instead of ad hoc tests, and finding a critical path in a timing report
  • Teamwork: agreeing on signal names and module interfaces first, then working on modules separately, and merging with short-lived branches and pull requests

Limitations

The hardware-scheduled design misses the 20 ns clock constraint by 5.43 ns because one cycle covers forwarding, data memory, the ALU, and the next-PC logic. Resolving branches earlier or using a carry-lookahead adder would shorten it, and there is no branch prediction.

Resources used

  • Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design: RISC-V Edition; the course toolflow and lectures
  • Repositories: single-cycle, software-scheduled pipeline, hardware-scheduled pipeline

Quantized CNN inference in C++

CourseCPRE 4870/5870, Lab 4, September 27 – October 5, 2026
Team2 people; the Lab 4 work in the repository is mine
StackC++, Python, TensorFlow/Keras, Jupyter, Make
Result8-bit model 4× smaller and 1.6× faster than fp32 with the same accuracy

Description of project

An embedded target has far less memory than a desktop and no fast floating point. We took a TinyImageNet CNN from earlier labs (a C++ framework that we first checked against TensorFlow, then a hardware multiply-accumulate unit) and converted it after training to 8-, 4-, and 2-bit integers in the same C++ code base, then measured size, speed, and accuracy on 1,000 validation images.

The starting point was Lab 2, where our C++ reimplementation matched TensorFlow to within 2.4 × 10−7. A single inference took 147 ms on the lab machine and 2.27 s on the ZedBoard's ARM core, and the second convolution layer alone used 62% of the time.

Storage
773 KB
Latency per image
87.6 ms
Top-1 accuracy
23.8%
Show the data table
ModelStorageLatencyTop-1Top-10
fp323,081 KB142.9 ms23.5%60.5%
8 bit773 KB87.6 ms23.8%60.4%
4 bit773 KB87.6 ms6.6%24.1%
2 bit773 KB87.8 ms0.3%4.6%

8 bits keeps accuracy, 4 bits loses most of it, and 2 bits is at chance level. At 2 bits, activations after the second convolution round to zero and the network outputs a constant.

My role

  • Profiled weight and activation ranges on 1,000 training images
  • Wrote the export script that computes each layer's scale and zero-point and writes int8 weights and int32 biases
  • Added the integer inference path to the C++ framework behind one build flag, plus a validation mode and the script that exports the 1,000 images
  • Wrote the report. In the earlier labs of this series, I worked on the layer implementation and measured performance in Lab 2, and wrote the on-board test suite and performance measurements for the MAC units in Lab 3, while my teammate wrote most of the MAC VHDL.

Skills or knowledge gained

  • How scale and zero-point map a real range onto integers, and why accumulation must happen in 32 bits before requantizing for the next layer
  • That outliers set the scale: one dense-layer weight near −1.32 stretches the range for all the others
  • That memory is more than weights: reusing two activation buffers made the 8-bit model fit a 1,000 KB budget
  • Making results reproducible on three machines with one repository and one build flag, and stating which numbers were measured and which calculated

Limitations

The 4- and 2-bit values sit in 8-bit containers, so they save neither space nor time until bit-packing is added. The base model is weak (23.5% top-1), which limits what the comparison can show. Latency was measured on a desktop CPU; the board numbers come in the next lab.

Resources used

  • Sze, Chen, Yang and Emer, Efficient Processing of Deep Neural Networks; the course DNN framework and lab handouts; the four lab reports are linked on the Experience and presentations page
  • Repositories: Lab 4 (quantization), Lab 2 (C++ framework), Lab 3 (MAC units)

Android social app for finding people and groups

CourseCOM S 3090, Software Development Practices, January to May 2026
Team4 students: two on the Spring Boot backend, two on the Android frontend (I was one of the two on the frontend)
StackJava, Android Studio, Volley, WebSocket, Spring Boot, Gradle, Espresso and JUnit, GitLab CI/CD
ResultA working Android app connected to the production server, with system tests and a coverage report

Description of project

Even on one campus it is hard to find people or clubs who share your interests. Our app lets students browse profiles, match, and move into group chats built around hobbies. It has three kinds of users: students (profile, swipe, match, join groups, report), group moderators (approve or remove members and handle reports), and administrators (approve sign-ups and manage reports and accounts).

The Android app talks to a Spring Boot server over REST and WebSocket. The backend covers users, matches, groups, group members, conversations, messages, notifications, reports, and user images.

My role

I worked on the Android frontend, with more than 100 commits over the term.

  • February: Volley request experiments (string, JSON, image), the sign-up and delete-account screens, and the first round trip with the backend.
  • March: group create, read, update, and delete; membership management (join requests, approve, ban, moderator toggle); the match list with accept, decline, and block; and a WebSocket notification screen.
  • April: interest-based group search and recommendation tabs, a real-time notification banner, the report system with a moderator panel, the frontend CI/CD pipeline, and Javadoc.
  • May: the admin dashboard and its role-based flow (sign-up, approval, login), Android system tests, and the coverage report.
  • For group recommendation I designed the frontend first, then wrote the API specification the backend needed. Teammates built the Spring Boot backend and the chat, swipe, and login screens.

Skills or knowledge gained

  • Android activities and XML layouts, REST calls with Volley, and mapping JSON fields
  • Receiving real-time events through a WebSocket listener and manager
  • Espresso system tests, coverage measurement, and a GitLab CI/CD pipeline for an app
  • Developing against a mock server (Mockoon) before the real endpoints exist
  • Teamwork: writing down the API I needed, reconciling field names with the backend, feature branches and merge requests, and agreeing on scope before each demo with screen sketches and a block diagram

Limitations

The server address is written into individual activities, so changing environments meant editing many files; it should be one configuration value. The notification stack worked on the frontend, but a matching backend change was still pending at the end of the term. The response-time targets in the requirements (0.5 s for UI actions, 2 s for sign-in) were never measured, and location-based discovery and group events were not built.

Resources used

  • The course tutorials repository (Android, Volley, WebSocket, Spring Boot examples), Android developer documentation, Mockoon, and Postman
  • Repository: coms3090-2_sc_2, a preserved copy of the course GitLab repository with all branches

React and Node.js web apps: SkillFlix and an aircraft API

CourseCOM S 3190, Construction of User Interfaces, September to December 2025
Team2 students (team NM_15)
StackHTML and CSS; React, React Router, and Tailwind CSS; Node.js, Express, and MongoDB
ResultA course-enrollment single-page app, and a REST API that the course's React interface runs against end to end

Description of project

Three assignments built on each other. Assignment 1 was a product catalog in plain HTML and CSS from a provided page skeleton. Assignment 2, SkillFlix, is a single-page course platform styled like a streaming service: horizontally scrolling category rows, a course details page with a video, an enrollment form with live validation, and a simulated payment and confirmation screen. It reads its courses from a JSON file and works on mobile.

In Assignment 3 the course staff gave us a finished React interface wired to an API that did not exist, and our job was to build that API. We wrote an Express server with routers and controllers for routes, aircraft, and airports, backed by a MongoDB connection.

My role

  • Assignment 1: the FAQ page and its custom CSS.
  • Assignment 2: the Home (browse courses) and enrollment form views, including loading the JSON data, form validation, and the responsive Tailwind layout. My partner built the course details and payment views.
  • Assignment 3: finished the aircraft controller (create, read, update, delete, and the routes assigned to an aircraft), did the final integration pass against the frontend, wrote the backend README, and recorded the submission video. My partner set up the database connection and server and wrote the route controller.

Skills or knowledge gained

  • Breaking a page into reusable React components, passing data as props, and holding state with useState and useEffect
  • Form validation that reports errors for each field before submission, and responsive layout with Tailwind
  • Structuring an Express API as routers that map URLs to controller functions, and using the MongoDB driver directly
  • Building to a fixed contract: the provided frontend defined the API, so every disagreement had one right answer, and I debugged against a UI I did not write
  • The GitLab flow: issue-numbered branches, merge requests, and reverting a mistaken commit

Limitations

SkillFlix has no backend, so enrollments are not saved and payment is simulated. For Assignment 1, the finished FAQ work is on a separate branch and was not merged into main. The Assignment 3 API has no automated tests (I verified it by hand through the UI), no authentication or input validation, and its seed data must be imported by hand with MongoDB Compass.

Resources used

  • MDN Web Docs, Express and MongoDB driver documentation, course lectures, and the provided starter files and frontend
  • Repositories: Assignment 1, Assignment 2 (SkillFlix), Assignment 3 (aircraft API)

Reflections

Cumulative reflection

I chose Computer Engineering because I wanted to be a web developer. My sophomore year, I struggled to adapt to the pace and stress of university coursework, and my grades showed it. Over a break I rebuilt the college math I was missing and changed how I study.

Instead of memorizing before exams, I now tie each concept to an assignment or lab, and I explain it to classmates in the same course. Simplifying an idea well enough to teach it forces me to understand it completely. Once I committed to my major coursework, I found that I actually liked engineering, and hardware most of all, starting with Digital Logic and EE 201 and growing through computer architecture and embedded systems.

Building a pipelined RISC-V processor in CPRE 3810 showed me how a computer really works, and the machine-learning labs in CPRE 4870 connected that to neural networks: where the multiply-adds are, and what precision a network can give up. Senior Design added a different side of the field, building a system with a team. I can finish labs, but I want to get better at independent technical judgment, starting a design with nothing in front of me. After graduation I plan to keep building personal projects and entering competitions to develop that.

General Education reflection

I went to school in Korea through high school, where learning centered on studying alone. At Iowa State I noticed how much more the education here relies on collaboration and teamwork, and that shift changed how I learn: some of my best understanding now comes from working with others and from explaining ideas to classmates. Tutoring taught me the same lesson from the teacher's side, since I had to find the explanation that worked for one particular person.

My study of facial recognition and surveillance in my ethics course showed me that engineering decisions reach well beyond the lab. A system that works technically can still harm people's privacy, and I want the technology I help build to advance alongside the social questions it raises.

Before Technical Communication (ENGL 3140), my presentations were loose: I described a concept or the results of an experiment and left it there. In this course I chose a technical topic of my own and had to present it in a set structure and a formal format. Organizing it that way showed me what I didn't yet understand, and my grasp of the technology improved because I had to explain it completely and in order. That experience changed how I think about communication: a clear structure is a tool for understanding, not only for delivery. I see it in my own work now. The README for our quantization lab includes the exact build commands and a results table so a reader can reproduce and judge what we did, and the project summaries in this portfolio are written for someone who has never seen my code.

Growing up in one educational culture and finishing my degree in another also taught me to adapt: to read how a new group works, ask for help, and give it. Those skills matter as much as any circuit I design, because hardware is built by teams.

Ethics paper

Engineering Ethics Case Study · CPRE 2320, Professional and Ethical Issues in Electrical and Computer Engineering · Fall 2025

Summary of the paper

A look at engineers' responsibility in China's mass facial recognition system. I examined the facial recognition surveillance network built in China, focusing less on the government than on the engineers who build and maintain it: what they owe their employer, the public, and their own conscience.

I combined two frameworks. Utilitarianism weighs the system's claimed security benefits against its harms, and the IEEE Code of Ethics judges the engineers' professional conduct on public safety, avoiding harm, and fairness. Utilitarianism did not justify the system: the loss of privacy, the chilling effect on speech, and the persecution of minority groups outweigh a small drop in crime. The IEEE Code points to specific failures, such as ignoring measured bias in the algorithm and designing data collection with no consent or opt-out.

I compared three options (an engineering boycott, an independent audit with strictly restricted use, and de-identifying all data) and recommended the audit, with the boycott and de-identification as fallbacks if the audit fails. I also argued that both frameworks have limits: utilitarianism struggles to put a number on freedom, and the IEEE Code has no enforcement power for an engineer who faces legal risk.

What I took from it is that technology is never neutral, and that engineers need to decide in advance where their line is.
